      "status_by_id": "rc:2627688908",

      "status": "fixed",
      "status_note": "author eliminated preprocessor checks and include weirdness in later rework",

      "text": "Why load multiple words across two blocks into SIMD vectors rather than holding the same word across multiple blocks?",

claims.text: ChaCha20 produced incorrect output on big-endian platforms
claims.quote: My biggest objection currently is that it's broken on big-endian systems - left a suggestion how to reproduce and fix it.
claims.status_note: author pushed big-endian fix suggested by l0rinc

claims.text: The generic vectorized implementation is roughly 2x slower than scalar on ARM64 when compiled with GCC
claims.quote: RPi5 with GCC shows a regression: the generic vectorized implementation is ~2x slower than scalar on ARM64 with GCC, while Clang handles it fine.
claims.status_note: author refactored to a 128-bit vector implementation to work around GCC vectorizer limitation
claims.status_by_quote: The second introduces a pluggable vector interface, and adds a 128bit implementation. This works around gcc's vectorizer

claims.text: A circular include dependency between chacha20_vec and chacha20_vec_128impl fails CI dependency linting
claims.quote: Note that the CI indicates a dependency-cycle regression was introduced here.

claims.text: Corecheck measures the 64-byte vector case about 7% slower than scalar code
claims.quote: Corecheck currently has no coverage data for the new code and measures the 64-byte case about 7% slower.

claims.text: IBD with V2 transport was considerably slower with this PR on Umbrel compared to master
claims.quote: master V1 and V2 were basically the same, while this PR was considerably slower there

claims.text: Cover all dispatch block counts with unit tests, isolated benchmarks, and extended differential fuzzing
claims.quote: To be more confident in the correctness, I would like to see the new path covered by: tests... focused benchmarks... extension of the existing crypto_diff_fuzz_chacha20 target

claims.text: Why separate this into an .ipp file if it is only included in a single .cpp file?
claims.quote: Why separate this into an .ipp file if it's only included in a single .cpp file?
claims.status_note: author explained that future runtime-detected implementations require separate compilation flags
claims.status_by_quote: some impls may require different compilation flags (-mavx2/-mavx512vl), which have to be in their own compilation units.

claims.text: Use static constexpr bools and if constexpr instead of preprocessor #if !defined blocks
claims.quote: Using `#if !defined` for these seems old school. Why not static constexpr bools, and `if constexpr (..)`?
claims.status_note: author agreed if constexpr makes sense where possible
claims.status_by_quote: if constexpr certainly makes more sense where possible. I'll have a look, thanks!

claims.text: Add a static_assert checking sizeof(vec256) == 32
claims.quote: static_assert(sizeof(vec256) == 32) ?
claims.status_note: author declined explaining accesses use operator[], reviewer clarified it protects against compilers ignoring vector attributes
claims.status_by_quote: Sorry, I meant just so you get an error if you're using a compiler ignores the __attribute__ entirely

claims.text: Add explanatory comments detailing the inverted quarterround SIMD round logic
claims.quote: Could use a little more explanation in the comment I think? But makes sense to me.
claims.status_note: author agreed to add context in comments
claims.status_by_quote: Sure, I can definitely add some more context

claims.text: Was this tested on big-endian systems that do not fall back to scalar code?
claims.quote: quick question before I do: was it tested on any big-endian systems which don't revert to non-vectorized run?
claims.status_note: author clarified big-endian support was best-effort and untested
claims.status_by_quote: I forgot to mention in the PR description that big-endian was best-effort and untested.

claims.text: Use existing internal_bswap_32 helpers rather than __builtin_bswap32
claims.quote: can we assume that all big endian systems have `__builtin_bswap32` available? https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/blob/432b18ca8d0654318a8d882b28b20af2cb2d2e5d/src/compat/byteswap.h#L14-L16 indicates we could use our existing helpers here instead
claims.status_by_quote: Thanks, yes, I meant to change that to internal_bswap_32 before pushing. Will do.

claims.text: Use simple fixed-bound runtime loops instead of recursive templates for unrolling
claims.quote: Hmmm, it seems to me we're doing heavy recursive templates here to unroll loops... Can you please try if this also works and results in the same speedup?
claims.status_note: author benchmarked and showed runtime loops and helper abstractions caused severe regressions due to missing inlining and unrolling
claims.status_by_quote: Ok, after some experimenting, I am very hesitant to add the helpers as suggested above.

claims.text: Use ALWAYS_INLINE defined in attributes.h instead of redefining it locally
claims.quote: Could we use https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/blob/e16c22fe025f82166c7f3f15a37c96bf4a06e4cf/src/attributes.h#L19-L25 instead?
claims.status_note: author agreed initially but reviewer noted later in rc:3887632159 that it remains locally redefined
claims.status_by_quote: Is there a specific reason for redefining ALWAYS_INLINE here?

claims.text: Use std::index_sequence compile-time loops instead of recursive templates
claims.quote: I believe it's possible to use compile-time loops here instead of recursive templates (if runtime loops don't get optimized sufficiently)
claims.status_note: author noted they will experiment with index_sequence unrolling
claims.status_by_quote: The index_sequence trick is neat. If that ends up looking cleaner/more obvious than the recursive iteration, that works for me. I'll play around with it.

claims.text: Add a short description explaining that the crypt function peels off larger blocks first before finishing smaller blocks
claims.quote: I think this function should get a short description too. Wasn't immediately clear to me that it attempts to peel off larger blocks first before potentially finishing with a few smaller blocks.

claims.text: Why load multiple words across two blocks into SIMD vectors rather than holding the same word across multiple blocks?
claims.quote: Intuitively I would have expected that the vectors hold the same word spread over multiple blocks. But if I understand your approach here, we have multiple words over two blocks. Is it just easier to express the quarter rounds in this way?

claims.text: Guard feature macros before using them and restrict targets to x86_64 and aarch64
claims.quote: Now that we're relying on `__builtin_shufflevector` after the GCC codegen issues (and since we only enable this on `x86_64`, `amd64`, and `aarch64`), should we guard the feature macros before using them?

claims.text: Pass state as a fixed-extent span, dispatch vector groups at the start of ChaCha20Aligned::Crypt, and let the existing scalar loop handle remainders
claims.quote: Could we pass the state as a fixed-extent span, dispatch vector groups at the start of `ChaCha20Aligned::Crypt`, and let its existing scalar loop process the remainder?

claims.text: Extract target loops into named helpers and use a switch statement for exact group counts
claims.quote: Could we move each target loop into a named helper, express exact group counts with `switch`, and leave the entry point only to select one constexpr target?

claims.text: Add benchmarks for boundary sizes (128, 192, 768-960 bytes) and BIP324 sizes (318-320 bytes)
claims.quote: Instead of documenting how each platform behaved... could we cover those four boundary sizes?

claims.text: Expose the backend's minimum block count to skip constructing vector state on short calls that fall back to scalar
claims.quote: The AArch64 backend handles 4 or more blocks, yet 1-3-block `Crypt` calls still construct its vector state before returning to scalar code. Could we expose the backend's minimum block count and skip shorter calls consistently

claims.text: Derive input size in crypto_diff_fuzz_chacha20 from blocks [0, 100] plus tail bytes [0, 63] to test every vector group
claims.quote: Could we derive the input size from named `blocks` in `[0, 100]` plus `tail_bytes` in `[0, BLOCKLEN - 1]`?

claims.text: Is 15 blocks faster than 8+7 on Apple Silicon?
claims.quote: Is 15 also faster than e.g. 8+7? On my M4 Max, processing 14 and 15 blocks as 8+6 and 8+7 is faster than using exact 14- and 15-state groups.

claims.text: Rename the TU to chacha20_vec_dispatch.cpp to resolve the CI dependency lint cycle
claims.quote: Could we rename this TU to `chacha20_vec_dispatch.cpp`, include `chacha20_vec.h` from the implementation header, and keep one definition of `BLOCKLEN` and `STATE_WORDS`?

claims.text: Extend test vectors to cover and compare the new vector specializations
claims.quote: It seems to me the existing standard test vectors are too short (mostly < 128 bytes) to trigger the vectorized optimization - can we extend the tests to runa and compare the new specializations

claims.text: Add comments documenting compiler versions and architectures that failed to inline lambdas efficiently
claims.quote: Could we get some comments in the code as to compiler versions (and architecture) that failed to be efficient enough with lambdas
claims.status_note: author agreed to add more context
claims.status_by_quote: Sure, I can definitely add some more context and clean up the wonky variable names.

claims.text: Is there a particular reason for avoiding the existing approach?
claims.quote: Is there a particular reason for the aversion to the current approach? It seems easier to read and probably also to debug to me.

claims.text: Expose target minimums of two blocks on x86-64 and three on AArch64, leaving shorter calls scalar
claims.quote: Corecheck measures the one-block vector path slower, while CryptStates<3> improved the 192-byte median from 0.98 to 0.86 ns/byte on this Apple M4 Max. Could we expose target minimums of two blocks on x86-64 and three on AArch64, and leave shorter calls scalar?
